title: Node.js Event Loop and Concurrency Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of Node's single-threaded model, libuv, the event loop phases, the ordering of nextTick, setImmediate and setTimeout, how to avoid blocking the loop, and when to use worker threads.

chapters.title: Single-Threaded Model and Mental Model
points: Node runs your JavaScript on one main thread: one call stack, one callback runs at a time, so there are no data races on plain JS variables
Node is single-threaded for JS only: libuv, the OS kernel and a thread pool do the I/O and heavy work in the background
Mental model: the stack runs sync code, then the event loop picks finished-work callbacks from queues and pushes them onto the stack one at a time
Good for I/O-bound work (many sockets, little CPU); bad for CPU-bound work because one slow callback delays every other request
Interview Point: Is Node really single-threaded? How does it handle 10k concurrent connections? Why is CPU-heavy work a problem for it?

chapters.title: libuv and the Event Loop Phases
points: libuv is the C library under Node that provides the event loop, async network I/O (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) and the thread pool
Phase order per loop turn: timers → pending callbacks → idle/prepare → poll → check → close callbacks
timers runs expired setTimeout/setInterval callbacks; poll retrieves new I/O events and runs their callbacks; check runs setImmediate; close runs socket.on('close')
Thread pool: default size 4 (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE), used for fs, dns.lookup, crypto (pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes) and zlib; TCP/UDP sockets do not use it
Interview Point: Name the event loop phases in order. Which operations use the thread pool and which do not? What does the poll phase do when no timers are due?

chapters.title: nextTick vs setImmediate vs setTimeout
points: process.nextTick runs right after the current operation, before the loop continues and before promise microtasks; the nextTick queue drains first, then the microtask queue
setImmediate runs in the check phase of the current loop turn; setTimeout(fn, 0) runs in the timers phase of a later turn (0 is clamped to 1ms)
From the main module, setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate order is non-deterministic; inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always fires first
Example order in a CommonJS file: sync code → nextTick → promise .then → setTimeout/setImmediate (console.log in that order proves it); in an ES module the promise logs before nextTick
Interview Point: Why can recursive nextTick starve I/O? Predict the output order of nextTick, Promise.then, setTimeout and setImmediate. When is setImmediate deterministic?

chapters.title: Blocking the Event Loop
points: Blocking means a callback runs long synchronously, so timers, requests and I/O callbacks all wait and latency spikes for every client
Typical culprits: fs.readFileSync or other *Sync calls in handlers, JSON.parse/stringify of huge payloads, ReDoS-prone regex, big loops, sync crypto
Fixes: use async APIs, split work into chunks yielding with setImmediate, offload to a worker thread or child process
Detect it with event loop delay monitoring (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay) or --cpu-prof; sustained high p99 delay means a blocked loop
Interview Point: How would you find what is blocking the loop? Why is a sync call at startup fine but not in a request handler? How do you break up a long loop?

chapters.title: Worker Threads for CPU-Bound Work
points: worker_threads runs JS in a separate thread with its own V8 isolate, event loop and memory: new Worker('./job.js', { workerData })
Communicate with parentPort.postMessage and worker.on('message'); data is copied by structured clone, ArrayBuffers can be transferred, and SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics shares memory
Comparison: worker threads share a process and are light; child_process is a separate process with IPC; cluster forks processes to use all cores for request handling
Use a worker pool (for example piscina) instead of spawning per task; do not use workers for I/O, since async I/O is already non-blocking
Interview Point: When use worker_threads vs cluster vs child_process? How do workers share data? Why can spawning a worker per request hurt?

chapters.title: Node Concurrency Cheat Sheet
points: Loop turn: timers → pending → idle/prepare → poll → check → close; nextTick and microtasks run between callbacks
Priority: sync code > process.nextTick > promise microtasks > setTimeout/setImmediate
Thread pool: 4 threads by default, set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE before start-up; covers fs, dns.lookup, crypto, zlib, not sockets
Never in handlers: *Sync calls, huge JSON.parse, catastrophic regex; chunk with setImmediate or offload to worker threads
Interview Point: Summarise how Node serves many clients on one thread. What would you check first for high latency under CPU load? How do you scale across cores?
